items.title: Developing Critical AI Literacy Through Student-AI Dialogue in Engineering Education
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence tools into higher education has created a critical paradox: students engage with AI daily yet rarely develop the skills to evaluate, question, or challenge AI-generated content. This paper presents the Cognitive Bridge methodology — a pedagogical framework developed and implemented at the National Polytechnic University of Armenia (NPUA) over nearly two years of iterative research and classroom practice (2024– 2026) — designed to transform AI from a passive answer-generator into an active cognitive challenge for engineering students. Grounded in Bloom's Revised Taxonomy and Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), the methodology positions AI as a deliberately imperfect cognitive partner whose errors and limitations become the productive substance of learning. Over a four-week quasi-experimental intervention involving approximately 150 engineering students, participants progressed from intuitive AI use (Week 1 baseline) through guided error-detection and critical questioning (Weeks 2–3) to independent AI auditing (Week 4). Findings are supported by a parallel anonymous survey of N=149 engineering students on AI ethics awareness, revealing moderate AI literacy (Q10: M=3.29/5; Q11: M=3.34/5) alongside critically low knowledge of the EU AI Act (Q12: M=2.27/5). Qualitative thematic analysis identified three dominant themes: AI dependency as the primary ethical concern, university responsibility for structured instruction, and spontaneous student recognition of the Cognitive Bridge instruction in anonymous surveys. Results suggest that structured, longitudinal AI-challenge pedagogy significantly develops critical thinking, verification habits, and ethical awareness, offering a scalable, low-cost model applicable across diverse institutional contexts.

items.title: DMAIC, Augmented: Generative AI Strengthens Lean Six Sigma Execution
items.abstract: This article examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI) assistants can strengthen Lean Six Sigma (LSS) execution across every phase of the Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control (DMAIC) methodology. The objective is to give LSS practitioners field-tested patterns, quantified cycle-time data, and a governance framework for integrating AI assistants into quality-improvement projects without compromising methodological rigor. The investigation draws on recent industry deployments using Anthropic’s Claude assistant and a construct called skills: versioned playbooks that bundle written instructions, scripts, reference data, and validation rules into reusable artifacts. Methods include direct measurement of cycle-time deltas across Define, Measure, and Control tasks; four worked Analyze-phase examples spanning hypothesis testing, Measurement System Analysis, Statistical Process Control, and regression interpretation; and analysis of a multi-skill portfolio deployed at a small aviation services client. Results demonstrate substantial efficiency gains: project-charter drafting time fell from 90 to 120 minutes to roughly 6 minutes; monthly payroll consolidation fell from 90 minutes to under 30 seconds (a 99.4 percent reduction) with the first-pass error rate dropping to zero; cross-system benefits reconciliation fell from 4 hours to under 60 seconds, with monthly completion improving from 5 of 12 cycles to 12 of 12. The aggregate skills portfolio at one client achieved approximately 84 hours of administrative cycle-time savings per year. The article identifies six required governance controls (human review, version control, controlled prompts, sensitive-data boundaries, hallucination mitigation, and auditability) and aligns them with ISO 9001: 2015 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The conclusion is that generative AI does not alter DMAIC methodology; it lowers the cost of executing each phase well, expanding the share of LSS that is practiced in fact rather than only in theory. The findings support Master Black Belts and quality champions in deliberately piloting AI-enabled tooling, prioritizing Control-phase tasks first, and treating skill development as a formal deliverable with version control, ownership, and quality gates.

items.abstract: EPT E INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFIOS E POSSIBILIDADES PARA A FORMAÇÃO DE PROFISSIONAIS NA ERA DIGITAL. VOCATIONAL AND TECHNOLOGICAL EDUCATION AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CHALLENGES AND POSSIBILITIES FOR PROFESSIONAL TRAINING IN THE DIGITAL AGE. EDUCACIÓN PROFESIONAL Y TECNOLÓGICA E INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFÍOS Y POSIBILIDADES PARA LA FORMACIÓN DE PROFESIONALES EN LA ERA DIGITAL. Gabriel Nascimento de Carvalho Simone Helen Drumond Ischkanian Gladys Nogueira Cabral Celine Maria de Sousa Azevedo Silvana Nascimento de Carvalho Sygride Nascimento de Carvalho Sandro Garabed Ischkanian RESUMO A Educação Profissional e Tecnológica (EPT) enfrenta desafios relacionados à incorporação da inteligência artificial nos processos de ensino e aprendizagem, na organização curricular e no desenvolvimento de competências necessárias ao mundo do trabalho. A expansão das tecnologias digitais demanda reflexões sobre as possibilidades de inovação pedagógica, a preparação dos docentes, a formação crítica dos estudantes e as implicações éticas do uso de sistemas inteligentes. Diante desse cenário, estabelece-se como problema de pesquisa: de que maneira a inteligência artificial pode contribuir para a formação de profissionais na EPT, considerando as exigências da transformação digital e os desafios de sua implementação educacional? O objetivo geral consiste em analisar os desafios e as possibilidades da integração da inteligência artificial à formação profissional, com atenção às competências técnicas, digitais, críticas e éticas requeridas na contemporaneidade. Metodologicamente, propõe-se uma pesquisa qualitativa, de caráter exploratório e descritivo, desenvolvida por meio de revisão bibliográfica e análise documental de publicações científicas e documentos institucionais pertinentes à temática. A análise permite discutir possibilidades de personalização da aprendizagem, apoio às atividades pedagógicas, simulação de situações profissionais e aproximação entre educação e transformações tecnológicas. Também evidencia desafios relativos à infraestrutura, à formação docente, à proteção de dados, aos vieses algorítmicos e às desigualdades de acesso. Conclui-se que a integração da inteligência artificial à EPT requer planejamento pedagógico, formação continuada e princípios éticos, de modo a articular inovação tecnológica, inclusão educacional e desenvolvimento humano na preparação dos profissionais para a era digital. Palavras-chave: Educação profissional e tecnológica; inteligência artificial; formação profissional; competências digitais. ABSTRACT Professional and Technological Education (PTE) faces challenges related to the incorporation of artificial intelligence into teaching and learning processes, curriculum organization, and the development of skills required in the world of work. The expansion of digital technologies calls for reflection on the possibilities of pedagogical innovation, teacher preparation, students’ critical development, and the ethical implications of using intelligent systems. Against this background, the research problem is formulated as follows: how can artificial intelligence contribute to professional training in PTE, considering the demands of digital transformation and the challenges of its educational implementation? The general objective is to analyze the challenges and possibilities of integrating artificial intelligence into professional education, focusing on the technical, digital, critical, and ethical competencies required in contemporary society. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive approach, based on a literature review and documentary analysis of scientific publications and institutional documents relevant to the topic. The analysis discusses opportunities for personalized learning, support for pedagogical activities, simulation of professional situations, and closer alignment between education and technological change. It also identifies challenges involving infrastructure, teacher training, data protection, algorithmic bias, and unequal access. The study concludes that integrating artificial intelligence into PTE requires pedagogical planning, continuing professional development, and ethical principles to connect technological innovation, educational inclusion, and human development in preparing professionals for the digital age. Keywords: Professional and technological education; artificial intelligence; professional training; digital competencies. items.title: Ethics by Configuration: AI Ethics Principles in Coding Agent Instructions
items.abstract: As AI coding agents become integral to software development, projects increasingly utilise configuration files, such as context files and skills, to govern agent behaviour. While AI ethics principles are widely used in research and policy, little is known about whether and how they are reflected when developers configure coding agents. We studied ethics principles in 40,079 configuration files across 8,893 GitHub repositories. Using a validated large language model (LLM) classification, we measured the prevalence of ethics-related statements, and qualitatively analysed 702 stratified samples across 679 files to uncover the ethical considerations reflected in these files and the parties they concern. Ethics-related statements appeared in 39.4% of files and 61.5% of repositories; concentrated on accountability, transparency, privacy protection, and reliability; and occurred more often in task-specific files such as skills than in project-wide context files. Our qualitative analysis identified 30 categories of ethical considerations, which take the form of concrete rules for the agent. Accountability appeared mainly as requirements for human approval, transparency as explain and honestly report the agent's work, and fairness as accessibility and localisation. These considerations reveal a difference in focus. Whereas public ethics frameworks aim to protect society and end users, configuration files mainly concern developers, maintainers, and community members in the development workflow. Ethics-related content appeared mainly in prose-based files, and whether agents follow these instructions remains untested. We discuss the implications for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers.

items.title: Every scientist a modeller? The promise and peril of AI ‐assisted mechanistic models
items.abstract: Abstract Mechanistic models, expressed as simulations that can be run and visualised, are a powerful way to understand biological and other systems. Building them, however, requires formulating mathematical or rule‐based descriptions and translating them into working code, skills that many ecologists and other disciplinary researchers do not have. Generative AI can now perform much of this translation, making mechanistic modelling accessible to researchers, educators and students previously excluded by its technical demands. But delegating this translation to AI also carries real risks: modelling assumptions can become hidden, plausible but incorrect code can pass unnoticed, and the skills and critical habits that model building once developed may never form. We examine the benefits and risks of using generative AI as a modelling companion at each stage of model development (conceptual specification, formalisation, implementation and exploration), drawing on recent experimental evidence on AI‐assisted learning and on a worked predator–prey example built with AI, with a rule‐based epidemic model as a parallel case. At each stage we identify where consequential decisions are silently delegated to the AI and set out practical mitigations that keep human judgement engaged without requiring the technical skills AI has made optional: specifying the conceptual model explicitly before engaging AI, having the AI translate its formalisation back into plain language, testing the implementation against outcomes known from domain knowledge and designing the interface to support interrogation. This new opportunity is substantial: researchers, educators and students who understand their systems but have never been able to build models of them are now able to explore these systems mechanistically, testing how components interact and how the system responds to conditions it has not yet experienced, questions that correlative approaches alone cannot answer. Used carelessly, AI risks eroding modelling skill for little lasting benefit, but used deliberately, in the ways set out here, it opens a new pathway to mechanistic understanding without removing the critical thinking the old technical barrier once enforced.

items.title: Executive decision support for managing AI risk in public health
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming public health decision-making, shifting it from descriptive epidemiological reporting to predictive, accelerated operational guidance. Yet AI in public health is discussed almost entirely at technical or regulatory levels, leaving a gap in executive-level guidance. Public health operates within a complex landscape of social determinants, political scrutiny, and incomplete information, where algorithmic errors can severely damage public trust. Consequently, executive competency must expand beyond traditional data interpretation to foundational AI literacy. Leaders must differentiate among diverse AI applications and evaluate their risk profiles, including balancing AI trained on individual-level precision medicine models with public health population-level prevention mandate. Continuous human oversight and multidisciplinary validation should be standard for modern public health organizations. Automated systems must equitably advance population health outcomes under final human authority at all times. Public health executives can better prepare to make informed decisions about AI-related risks using the decision points presented in this commentary.

items.title: Exploring intentions to adopt GenAI in academia: perceived usefulness and attitudes among scholars and researchers
items.abstract: This study aims to investigate scholars’ and researchers’ perceptions, attitudes, and intentions toward using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic research. Employing a cross-sectional survey, data were collected from 1,283 participants in China. After removing missing values, 1150 valid responses were analyzed. Results indicate that perceived usefulness of GenAI was positively associated with attitudes (β = 0.489, p < 0.001) and directly associated with usage intention (β = 0.385, p < 0.001). Furthermore, attitudes toward GenAI had a positive effect on usage intention (β = 0.323, p < 0.001) and mediated the association between perceived usefulness and intention (indirect effect = 0.157, Boot95% CI [0.120, 0.199]). These findings underscore that positive perceptions of GenAI’s usefulness are associated with more favorable attitudes and stronger intentions to adopt it in research. By applying the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to GenAI adoption, this study highlights the need for academic institutions to promote responsible use through ethical guidelines, training programs, and awareness campaigns, which may facilitate effective integration into research practices.

items.title: Formal Explanations for Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces
items.abstract: Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces (LTLf) is widely used in Artificial Intelligence to specify desired temporal behavior and determine whether finite traces satisfy or violate it. Explaining these outcomes is essential for debugging and trust. However, existing approaches typically capture either sufficient reasons or counterfactual causes, without clarifying their relationship. We introduce a native characterization of abductive (AXps) and contrastive (CXps) explanations directly over finite traces, based on locking and unlocking time-indexed events. We prove its equivalence to the classifier-based formulation, and show that CXps coincide with a recently proposed temporal causality semantics for LTLf. This characterization enables an efficient implementation based on the enumeration of minimal unsatisfiable cores and minimal correction sets of ASP programs. Experiments on real-world event logs demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

items.title: From Agent Labels to Accountable Deployment: Evidence Maturity and Meaningful Human Oversight for Agentic AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence is entering higher education as systems progress from generating answers to planning and executing actions. This transition creates an ethical problem that aggregate accuracy cannot resolve: institutions may delegate consequential discretion before they possess evidence of durable benefit, fairness, or effective human control. This critical integrative review examines 15 peer-reviewed reviews, one recent preprint retained separately, and selected primary studies to determine what the evidence supports and what remains ethically unjustified. The literature is conceptually unstable, often conflating perceived agency, static generative AI, and systems with goal-directed execution. Evidence is strongest for bounded artifact quality and weakest for durable learning, equity, workload, and institution-level outcomes. Authentic deployments remain mostly short, single-site, and weakly connected to tested oversight arrangements. The article develops the Autonomy-Oversight-Evidence framework, comprising five autonomy levels, five oversight levels, and six stages of evidence maturity. Its normative principle is that delegated autonomy must not exceed either the maturity of the supporting evidence or the strength of accountable human oversight. This principle follows from duties to prevent avoidable harm, preserve learner autonomy, distribute risks fairly, maintain contestability, and keep institutional accountability with responsible persons. The framework converts these duties into reporting requirements, permission boundaries, approval checkpoints, logging, escalation, appeal, and rollback. Agentic AI may improve selected educational processes, but current evidence does not justify broad claims of sustained effectiveness or autonomous use in rights-affecting decisions.

items.title: From assistants to companions: An exploratory mixed-methods study of AI chatbot adoption among Generation Z students in Thailand
items.abstract: This study explores how undergraduate Generation Z students at an international college in Thailand adopt and use AI chatbots. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a sensitizing framework, we conducted an exploratory convergent mixed-methods survey of 144 eligible students. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics and exploratory factor analysis of seven adoption items adapted from TAM and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), while qualitative analysis used LLM-assisted, researcher-verified coding of 127 and 117 substantive open-ended responses to examine motivations and desired features. The analysis suggested two provisional adoption-related dimensions, perceived relational value and social endorsement, and practical accessibility, although the factor-retention criteria were divided between one and two factors. Almost all students selected academic assistance as a reason for using AI chatbots (92.4%). Asked specifically about AI companions, students most often cited information seeking and convenience (27.6% of substantive responses), while personal and emotional support and reservations about companion use were raised in 20.5% and 19.7% of responses, respectively. Human-like interaction was the most frequently requested feature category (39.3%), followed by technical capabilities and academic tools such as citation support. The study contributes exploratory, cross-sectional evidence on AI chatbot adoption in a Thai higher-education context and highlights the importance of balancing practical utility, relational expectations, and clear human-AI boundaries.

items.title: From Global Landscapes to Local Contexts: A Bibliometric Analysis of Artificial Intelligence and Student Behavior
items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications has profound implications for higher education,including student behaviors, engagement, and productivity in learning. While academic literature addressing the implications of AI applications is on the rise, its relevance for fields of economics, business,and the social sciences remains disparate and localized. In this regard, this paper analyzes the bibliometric landscape of AI research using a set of indicators that include keyword co-occurrence, time and research density, and emerging research fronts using VOSviewer, and the search was limited to Scopus-indexed journal articles (2000-2025).A descriptive analysis was done based on three sets of documents, namely the global baseline, the discipline-specific body of work,and a local Malaysian dataset. The global dataset has produced a mature and integrated network with a primary emphasis on educational data mining and learning analytics.Nevertheless, temporal overlay visualization analysis reveals a sharp transition to the human and ethical factors surrounding generative artificial intelligence, including academic integrity and frameworks for evaluating teacher acceptance of disruptive technologies. In contrast, the Malaysian dataset was found to have a sparsely connected network, suggesting the growing nature of local research. Indeed, studies pertaining to Malaysia appear to focus on the interactions between students and ChatGPT and lack psychological theories in any of the included works.This study has identified the fundamental disconnect between regional and international research practices.As such, it can serve as the foundation for future studies that seek to understand the effects of artificial intelligence on the emotional,social, and academic development of students in developed digital economies.

items.title: From Pilot to Production: A Seven-Check Readiness Framework for Deploying Generative and Agentic AI in the Enterprise
items.abstract: Many enterprise generative AI initiatives stall between a successful pilot and dependable production use. Industry forecasts suggest that at least 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept, and that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. This paper argues that the gap is primarily a management and delivery problem rather than a model-capability problem, and proposes a practitioner framework for go-live decisions. The framework rests on a single organizing analogy, treating an AI system like a new hire, and translates it into seven readiness checks (value, ownership, data, evaluation, guardrails, operations and adoption), six hard stops that block launch regardless of overall score, an eight-part evidence pack, a 0–2 scoring rubric, and an additional control set for agentic systems that can take actions. The checks are mapped to established sources including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, and empirical work on machine learning engineering. Seven publicly documented cases are used to illustrate the failure modes each check is designed to catch. The paper closes with limitations and a proposed agenda for empirical validation. JEL classification: M15, O32, O33.

items.title: From traditional employability skills to emerging AI competencies
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping graduate employability by changing how competencies are enacted, valued, and developed. While traditional employability frameworks identify competencies expected of graduates, limited research has examined how these competencies may be evolving within AI-enabled environments. This study examines established employability competency domains and explores faculty perceptions of emerging capability requirements in the age of generative AI. A sequential mixed-method design was adopted. Quantitative data from 177 graduating business students in Saudi Arabia were analysed using domain-level principal component analysis to assess the internal structure and reliability of seven established competency domains. Semi-structured interviews with twelve business faculty members were subsequently analysed thematically. The quantitative findings provide context-specific support for communication, leadership, critical thinking and problem-solving, teamwork, management capability, ICT capability, and professionalism. The qualitative findings identified three complementary patterns of perceived competency evolution: human-centric enduring competencies, AI-augmented competencies, and emerging AI-specific competencies. The findings suggest that AI-ready employability involves both the continuing relevance of established competencies and changes in how competencies are enacted alongside intelligent technologies. The study proposes an exploratory AI-ready employability framework integrating established competencies with perceived competency continuity, augmentation, and emergence, providing a foundation for further empirical investigation and curriculum development in AI-integrated higher education.

items.title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
items.abstract: Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market. Should an early-career researcher invest in a deep understanding of their field, or instead use AI to build a longer resume with many papers? Should a recruiter favor applicants with fewer papers who pass an interview aimed at probing understanding, or insist on both publication volume and a pass? In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model of this two-sided dilemma. We classify all pure-strategy equilibria that can arise in this game and use learning simulations to identify the behaviors that populations of applicants and recruiters may learn to adopt. Our analysis provides a framework for reasoning about how academic hiring can adapt to AI and for evaluating practices that preserve the value of deep understanding.

items.title: GenAI in Higher Education in the Context of East and South Asia: Current Trends and Stakeholders’ Perceptions
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education (HE) worldwide, yet evidence from Asia remains limited. This study examines how students, teachers, and other stakeholders in Asia perceive the role of GenAI in HE, identifying current usage trends and analysing how GenAI is incorporated into academic and pedagogical practices. Using a mixed methods design, the study gathered quantitative data through online surveys of undergraduate students and teachers. Qualitative insights were obtained through focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews with a sample of participants, including policymakers, educationists, I/NGO representatives, and IT sector professionals. Findings show that the research participants hold mixed views about the role of GenAI in HE, with some indications of integration into academic practices. The study provides insights into emerging GenAI practices in Asian HE and highlights implications for policy and pedagogical development.

items.title: Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
items.abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in learning enables students to delegate some cognitive processes to technology, a practice known as cognitive offloading. Although this practice may improve efficiency, using AI without critical evaluation may contribute to an illusion of competence, defined as a discrepancy between perceived understanding and actual performance. This study examined the relationship between AI-based cognitive offloading and the illusion of competence, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking among high school students in Makassar. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational design and purposive sampling were employed, involving 356 students aged 15–18 years. Cognitive offloading was measured using an adapted Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking using the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, and the illusion of competence through the discrepancy between Judgment of Learning and performance on an objective PISA-based test. Data were analyzed using Confirmatory Factor Analysis and path analysis in Mplus 8.4. The CFA results indicated acceptable measurement models for cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Path analysis showed that cognitive offloading was positively associated with the illusion of competence and negatively associated with critical thinking, while critical thinking was negatively associated with the illusion of competence. The significant indirect effect indicated complementary partial mediation. These findings highlight the importance of analyzing, evaluating, and verifying AI-generated output to support accurate judgments of understanding. ABSTRAK Penggunaan artificial intelligence (AI) generatif dalam pembelajaran memungkinkan pelajar menyerahkan sebagian proses kognitif kepada teknologi atau melakukan cognitive offloading. Meskipun meningkatkan efisiensi, penggunaan tanpa evaluasi kritis dapat menimbulkan illusion of competence, yaitu ketidaksesuaian antara keyakinan terhadap pemahaman dan performa aktual. Penelitian ini bertujuan menguji hubungan cognitive offloading berbasis AI dengan illusion of competence serta peran mediasi critical thinking pada pelajar SMA di Kota Makassar. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain cross-sectional correlational dan purposive sampling, melibatkan 356 pelajar berusia 15–18 tahun. Cognitive offloading diukur menggunakan adaptasi Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking menggunakan Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, sedangkan illusion of competence dioperasionalkan melalui ketidaksesuaian antara Judgment of Learning dan tes objektif berbasis PISA. Data dianalisis menggunakan Confirmatory Factor Analysis dan path analysis pada Mplus 8.4. Hasil CFA menunjukkan bahwa model pengukuran cognitive offloading dan critical thinking memiliki kesesuaian yang dapat diterima. Path analysis menunjukkan bahwa cognitive offloading berhubungan positif dengan illusion of competence dan negatif dengan critical thinking, sedangkan critical thinking berhubungan negatif dengan illusion of competence. Efek tidak langsung melalui critical thinking juga signifikan dan menunjukkan complementary partial mediation. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa kemampuan menganalisis, mengevaluasi, dan memverifikasi keluaran AI merupakan bagian penting dalam menjaga ketepatan pelajar ketika menilai pemahamannya.

items.title: Generation Is Cheap, Selection Is Sovereign
items.abstract: Generative AI has made plausible output abundant and cheap, but plausibility is not evidence and evidence is not authority. Leading AI assistants already concede this in the notice beneath every prompt box, telling users the system can make mistakes and asking them to check — handing the work of verification to individuals without instruments, records or authority. This working paper proposes Computational Trust Engineering (CTE), an engineering discipline for the path from a language model’s completion to an organization’s consequence. It separates three selections that current practice collapses into one: a generative selection (which continuation is probable?), an evidentiary selection (which candidate is supportable?) and an authority selection (may the supported candidate produce consequence?). CTE grounds these in four realities (human, AI, actual and governance reality) and treats familiar failure modes as measurable gaps between them. It frames evidentiary selection as metrology, with the individual claim as the counted unit, “unknown” as a legitimate result, calibrated instruments and traceable provenance. It introduces attention as the allocation of scarce measurement effort, and states when a language model may serve as an instrument. The paper defends the three-layer separation through collapse analysis and precedent from internal control, functional safety and metrology. It also maps CTE to the NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, ISO/IEC 42001, assurance cases and the EU AI Act, and closes with deployment postures, five falsifiable hypotheses and a research agenda.

items.title: Generative AI and AI literacy in Elementary Education: A Systematic Review of Research published from 2021 to January 2026
items.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI has influenced research on AI literacy education at the elementary school level. A systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted to study implementations of Generative AI and methods of AI literacy education in elementary education. The review data includes 211 studies published from 2021 to January 2026 identified from SCOPUS, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Taylor & Francis. Thematic content analysis was used to identify and analyze themes in the review data to examine how the research field has developed after the release of Generative AI technology. The analysis identifies fundamental issues affecting the implementation of Generative AI in elementary education, including concerns about human interaction, varying approaches to ethical questions, and frequent concerns regarding the reliability of Generative AI outputs. The definition of the ethical dimensions of critical AI literacy is found to be inconclusive, calling for a broader adoption of critical AI literacy education at the elementary school level. Established use cases of Generative AI are identified, especially with self-regulated learning and foreign language studies. A holistic and integrated approach to AI literacy education for students and pre-service teachers is supported by the analysis. This study identifies research gaps for longitudinal research on Generative AI in elementary schools, parents’ role in students’ AI literacy, and a need to reach a scholarly consensus on the definition of AI ethics.

items.title: Generative AI and legal practice: a complicated relationship
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely expected to transform professional practices across multiple sectors, including the legal profession. This article critically examines the growing integration of GenAI tools into legal work and the implications this development carries for professional competence, ethical responsibility, and the broader institutional structure of legal practice. While AI promises substantial gains in efficiency by automating tasks such as legal research, document drafting, information retrieval, and data analysis, their adoption also raises significant concerns regarding reliability, transparency, confidentiality, and professional accountability. While prevailing narratives surrounding AI adoption in law often frame technological integration as both inevitable and normatively desirable, emphasising efficiency and competitive advantage while downplaying potential risks and value conflicts, the increasing delegation of professional tasks to algorithmic systems challenges traditional understandings of legal expertise, particularly in relation to judgement, reasoning, and professional autonomy. Moreover, unequal access to advanced AI tools and proprietary datasets may reinforce structural inequalities within the legal market, benefitting larger firms while disadvantaging smaller practices. This article argues for a balanced approach that combines technological literacy with strong ethical frameworks and institutional safeguards. Ultimately, responsible integration of GenAI requires sustained human oversight and collective professional engagement to ensure that technological innovation supports, rather than undermines, the core values of legal practice.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration and Innovation in Corporate Communication Models: A Study of Intelligent Transformation Based on University-Industry-Research Collaboration
items.abstract: This study investigates how human-AI collaboration reshapes corporate communication models within intelligent transformation, focusing on university–industry–research collaboration as an enabling mechanism. Drawing on qualitative case evidence and framework development, the paper identifies three collaborative modes-co-design, adaptive integration, and evaluative feedback-that mediate between AI capabilities and organizational communication innovation. The findings suggest that successful intelligent transformation depends less on technology adoption than on the institutional alignment of academic knowledge, industrial practice, and research-driven experimentation. Corporate communication evolves from linear information dissemination to dynamic stakeholder engagement, with human oversight and ethical judgment embedded in AI-supported workflows. The paper contributes a framework linking university–industry–research inputs, human-AI collaboration modes, and communication performance, and concludes with implications for policy and managerial practice.

items.abstract: The authors investigated the impact of Artificial Intelligence on the personalized cosmetic shopping experience on the Shopee e-commerce platform in Viet Nam. The team proposed seven hypotheses examining how AI-related factors influence user satisfaction. A quantitative approach was used, with survey data collected from 229 respondents and analyzed via SPSS 22. Results indicate that five factors - Personalization Risk Management, Perceived Usefulness, Trust Level, Customer Behavior Recognition, and User Data Quality- have significant positive effects on user satisfaction. At the same time, the quality of Machine Learning Algorithms, when applied mechanically without domain-specific calibration, has a statistically significant negative effect. These findings contribute a novel empirical perspective on AI adoption in a high-involvement product category to offer practical recommendations for platform developers, cosmetic sellers, and regulatory authorities.

items.title: Impact of artificial intelligence on medical education: applications, benefits and challenges
items.abstract: This research explores the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on medical education, highlighting its applications, benefits, and challenges.AI has revolutionized medical teaching through tools such as advanced clinical simulations, intelligent tutoring systems, AI-assisted diagnostics, and automated assessments.These technologies enable personalized, safe, and efficient learning, enhancing the acquisition of clinical and diagnostic skills.Additionally, immediate feedback and the ability to practice in virtual environments without risking patient safety are significant benefits.However, the implementation of AI faces challenges such as data privacy, high costs, unequal accessibility, and the need for faculty training.The risk of technological dependency and the potential loss of essential soft skills in medical practice are also discussed.The essay concludes that while AI offers transformative opportunities, its integration must be carefully managed to ensure it complements, rather than replaces, human clinical judgment.The importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and ongoing research is emphasized to maximize the benefits of AI in medical education.

items.title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
items.abstract: We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent that we use for research on problems whose answers aprogram or data can check. Each candidate solution is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox; proposers see only a public score, and a private split decides what counts. The harness itself(prompts, tools, skills, playbook, meta agent) is an editable genome, changed only through a kernel-enforced gate with held-out and cost checks. An autonomous mode goes from a plain-text goal to a verified report with no human step: an agent picks an open problem and writes its verifier, the kernel calibrates it, an adversarial agent audits it, and an agent that never sees the verifier re-checks the result. Across fourteen problems in six days, for about $180 of model usage, the system produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information: a certified depolarizing-channel threshold point p = 0.064966, a qutrit positivity frontier of 0.2910672, a 44-gate depth-6 Golay state preparation, and a stabilizer-rank bound chi(T^7) <= 10. It also cut SABRE qubit-routing overhead from 68,559 to 12,087 added gates. In hardware, it cut the energy per MAC of an open 8x8 INT8 systolic tile by 77.7% through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow, bit-exact. Three fully autonomous runs ended in honestties with public records; one audit caught a stale record, and one agent-written score pointing the wrong way went unnoticed. We report the failures as carefully: the one self-derived harness generation was rejected on cost, proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and operator changes were decisive for several results.

items.title: LADDER: Diagnosing Domain-Level Self-Assessment Under Noisy Feedback
items.abstract: Knowing when they are reliable is essential for language models to support human-AI collaboration. Yet interaction feedback is not always complete or correct, and may mislead models' understanding of their own capabilities. We introduce LADDER to study how language models assess themselves under unreliable feedback. Our findings show that models can accurately report supplied performance information while still struggling to form trustworthy self-assessments from interaction experience. Apparently accurate assessments can obscure capability differences and do not necessarily predict future task performance. These findings suggest that trustworthy self-assessment should be evaluated against observed task performance and its predictive value. Our study provides empirical evidence of the limits of model self-knowledge and a basis for evaluating capability awareness in reliable human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Leadership as a Service? Delegating Leadership Functions to Agentic AI—Boundaries, Risks and Accountabilities
items.abstract: Leadership is increasingly delivered, in part, by software. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems now monitor team activity, coordinate work across people and tools, schedule and assign tasks, deliver feedback and performance nudges, and broker information between leaders and followers — functions that organisations once obtained only from human managers. This has prompted the suggestion that leadership itself is becoming a service: a set of functions that can be specified, subscribed to and supplied by systems rather than embodied in persons. This conceptual paper examines that suggestion critically. Drawing on functional leadership theory, the automation–augmentation paradox, and the literature on algorithmic management and trust in AI, I develop a function-by-delegability framework that classifies five leadership functions — sensing and monitoring, coordination, deciding and allocating, developing and giving feedback, and representing and meaning-making — according to how far each can responsibly be delegated to agentic systems. I argue that delegability is governed less by technical capability than by accountability: I introduce the accountability floor, the principle that functions whose delegation would break the chain of accountability may be automated in execution but never in ownership. I identify four risks of delegation — legitimacy and follower trust, bias at scale, accountability gaps, and erosion of the leadership pipeline — propose governance and design principles, and derive three propositions for empirical research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: LLM-Based Agentic AI in Manufacturing: A Scoping Review of Applications, System Designs and Evaluation Practices
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in manufacturing to design products, plan production, diagnose faults and operate equipment, but their designs and evaluations remain difficult to compare. We analyse 164 studies identified through Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore to examine manufacturing applications, agentic system designs and evaluation practices, and to identify where evaluation coverage falls short of the evidence that these task and design types would require. We propose taxonomies of applications, agentic designs and evaluation practices, and relate task and design characteristics to the evidence required to assess them. The findings reveal an imbalance between assessing output quality and verifying whether outputs satisfy manufacturing requirements. For planning and decision-making systems, executability and constraint compliance receive limited evaluation, while most evidence comes from offline data or simulation. Limited assessment of safety, stability across repeated runs and performance in industrial settings leaves a gap between demonstrated task performance and evidence of reliable operation under manufacturing conditions. The resulting taxonomies and evidence requirements help researchers select evaluations suited to each manufacturing use case and distinguish demonstrated task performance from evidence of reliable operation.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

items.title: LLM-Based Fuzzy Agent for Human–Machine Interaction in STEM Education and Taiwanese-English Co-Learning Application
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a Large Language Model (LLM)-based fuzzy agent framework designed to enhance Human-Machine Interaction (HMI) in Quantum Computational Intelligence (QCI) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) learning, as well as Taiwanese-English co-learning. By integrating QCI&AI STEM experiential learning with language co-learning applications, the framework creates an adaptive and personalized learning environment using fuzzy logic-based Human Intelligence (HI) and evolutionary computation-based Machine Intelligence (MI). The framework comprises three main components: (1) the QCI&AI STEM experiential learning agent, which integrates QCI software and AI-driven models to facilitate interactive STEM learning; (2) the Trustworthy AI Dialogue Engine (TAIDE)-based Taiwanese-English co-learning agent, which utilizes the Meta AI USTmodel, TAIDE, and fine-tuned Open AI Whisper-Taiwanese model for real-time Taiwanese-English co-learning; and (3) the fuzzy Knowledge Graph (KG) agent, which constructs teacher’s and learners’ knowledge graphs to evaluate the students’ learning performance. Besides, an HMI-based Observation with Comfortable Intelligence (HMI-OwCI) model is proposed to create intelligent technologies that are seamlessly integrated and intuitively aligned with human needs. Additionally, two supporting agents enhance the proposed framework: the Genetic Algorithm-based Neural Network (GANN) Agent, which optimizes QCI learning models, and the LLM fine-tuned agent, which refines Taiwanese-English co-learning and generates various Whisper-Taiwanese models. Experimental results highlight that GANN adapts well in QCI&AI STEM learning, Whisper-Taiwanesemodels generalize effectively, and the fuzzy KG agent enables adaptive learning assessments.

items.title: Mapping interdependencies among challenges to artificial intelligence adoption in drug discovery
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant potential to accelerate drug discovery, yet its adoption remains constrained by interdependent technical, organizational, and regulatory barriers. This study applies Fuzzy DEMATEL to analyze twelve challenges and uncover their causal structure using expert judgments expressed as triangular fuzzy numbers. Following normalization and CFCS defuzzification, Resistance to Change, Lack of Standardization, Limited Trust in AI Outputs, Talent Shortage, and Lack of Clinical Validation emerge as the primary causal drivers. These upstream barriers exert strong influence on downstream effects, including Regulatory Barriers, Biological Complexity, Integration with Legacy Systems, and Poor Data Quality. The findings indicate that several constraints commonly viewed as external are, in practice, manifestations of internal organizational and technical shortcomings. By providing a structured causal prioritization of barriers, this study offers actionable guidance for targeting high-leverage interventions in AI-enabled drug discovery. Findings reflect expert judgment within a North Cyprus context and should be interpreted as indicative organizational signals rather than universal prescriptions.

items.title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations
items.abstract: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems

items.title: MARQ: A Modular, LLM-Agnostic Requirement Quality Assessor Infused with Systems Engineering Knowledge
items.abstract: Requirements engineering (RE) is foundational to systems engineering (SE), as requirement defects can propagate downstream and adversely affect development outcomes. Although large language models (LLMs) are promising for requirement quality assessment, prior work shows that off-the-shelf models miss a large share of expert-identified defects, perform unevenly across quality criteria, and vary across executions. This study investigates whether infusing expert-derived SE knowledge can improve LLM-based requirement quality evaluation beyond off-the-shelf capability. We present MARQ, a modular, LLM-agnostic prototype that supplements LLMs with a criterion-specific knowledge stack operationalizing INCOSE requirement quality criteria and evaluated against off-the-shelf baselines on an expert-labeled NASA requirement set using Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the open-weight Gemma 3 12B, with 100 executions per model. MARQ achieves median F1 scores of 0.80 for Claude Opus 5, 0.62 for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 0.53 for Gemma 3 12B, compared with off-the-shelf baselines of 0.55, 0.52, and 0.18, respectively. However, the nature of these gains is model-dependent. Claude Opus 5 improves defect detection and false-alarm control; GPT-5.6 Sol gains detection and better execution-level consistency at the cost of more false alarms; and Gemma 3 12B reaches the performance of off-the-shelf proprietary models, although it remains highly variable. Criterion-level analysis shows gains concentrated in Correctness and Conformance, trade-offs between misses and false alarms within individual criteria, and model-dependent responses across several criteria. These findings position SE knowledge infusion as a promising model-agnostic pathway for strengthening trustworthy LLM-based RE support while underscoring the need for criterion-specific interventions and human-in-the-loop review.

items.title: Mathematics Teachers’ Pedagogical Evaluations of Artificial Intelligence in Mathematics Education: Opportunities, Risks, and Classroom Positioning
items.abstract: This study aimed to examine how mathematics teachers in public schools in Türkiye evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics teaching. The accuracy and pedagogical suitability of AI-generated content make such judgments important in mathematics education. Designed as a qualitative case study, the research focused on seven teachers drawn from a broader maximum variation sample. Participants varied in years of teaching experience, graduate education, and self-reported AI experience. Data were collected through semi-structured online interviews and analyzed using descriptive content analysis focused on teachers’ pedagogical reasoning. Codes were developed from the teachers’ statements and organized into categories of pedagogical opportunities, pedagogical and epistemic risks, and conditions of use. The findings indicated that teachers did not reject AI categorically; rather, they viewed it as a complementary tool whose value depended on teacher guidance, the mathematical accuracy and conceptual appropriateness of generated content, and alignment with instructional purposes. Lesson planning, individualized feedback, visualization, and time efficiency were identified as the main opportunities. Concerns included inaccurate content entering teaching and assessment, misconceptions, overreliance on ready-made answers, and reduced student participation in learning. Controlled use and teacher oversight were recurring criteria across different experience profiles. The study clarifies the subject-specific criteria mathematics teachers use when judging whether AI use is pedagogically acceptable.

items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM Behavior: A Survey
items.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain how internal computations produce large language model behaviors, yet findings remain fragmented across methods and behavioral domains. We survey 229 papers across five behavior families: epistemic, linguistic, reasoning, safety, and social behaviors. We introduce a framework distinguishing five levels of mechanistic evidence, from decodability to generalization. Our cross-behavior synthesis reveals recurring mechanisms, distinctions between representation and causal control, and limitations of existing explanations. We conclude by identifying gaps in understanding computational roles, behavioral interactions, and generalization to interactive and agentic settings.

items.title: Medical Embodied Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Delivery and Clinical Workflows
items.abstract: Medical embodied artificial intelligence (AI) closes the loop between sensing, action and feedback in clinical and care tasks, from procedures and examination to rehabilitation and hospital logistics. Its clinical value therefore depends not only on what a system can do, but on how its action loop fits the task, the people who supervise it and the service responsible for recovery. In this structured narrative Review, we trace the field from image-guided and teleoperated robots to learned policies and foundation models, and survey its technical foundations along the action loop, from perception and task reasoning to planning, control, vision–language–action and world models and safety monitoring, together with data and simulation resources and applications across eight clinical task categories. A 96-source evidence map and targeted technical searches underpin the synthesis, and a separately defined subset of 40 direct empirical studies characterises the settings in which embodied systems have been validated. Evidence in this subset remains predominantly preclinical or feasibility-based and does not establish clinical superiority or long-term safety. We argue that the principal translational bottleneck is not insufficient autonomy alone but a mismatch among task boundaries, machine authority, evidence maturity and health-service readiness. To address this mismatch, we propose a task-bounded framework that links the operational design domain and allocated authority to the evidence required, the conditions for implementation and the mechanisms for monitoring, revalidation and rollback, and we identify technical priorities in grounded foundation models, shared data, uncertainty-aware autonomy and verifiable safety. The framework prioritises clinically relevant comparators, effective clinician takeover and evaluation of the complete workflow, including preparation, supervision and recovery, and offers a basis for appraising deployment claims; its decision value and effects on care now require prospective evaluation.

items.title: MORAL RIGHTS OF AUTHORS IN THE AGE OF AI-GENERATED CONTENT
items.abstract: The technology of Generative AI is now capable not only of writing, painting, and composing, but even transforming the work of others. While India's Copyright Act, 1957 was framed taking humans into consideration as the creators, yet there is an exception for Computer Generated Works and an additional set of Moral Rights provided for in Section 57. The present article enquires into the possibility of using these provisions to safeguard the human creators in case AI transforms or creates a work. It contemplates that while the Copyright Act provides for a sufficient framework for the purpose, it lacks provisions regarding the role of humans in the creation, alteration by AI, misattribution, and proving the same. items.title: More Alerts, Less Prevention? A Computational Study of Hazard Detection, Response Capacity and Threshold Choice in Occupational Health and Safety
items.abstract: AI-enabled hazard detection is usually judged by whether it finds risky conditions. Prevention requires another step: somebody must have the time, authority and competence to respond. This article evaluates how that second step alters the interpretation of predictive safety performance. It reports a factorial computational experiment derived from a doctoral study of AI in occupational health and safety (OHS). Across 54 simulated operating conditions, five alert thresholds and 200 replications per condition, a score-based detector classifies 5,000 opportunities per replication. The design varies hazardous-opportunity prevalence (1%, 5% and 15%), score separation (1, 2 and 3), drift (0 and 0.75) and nominal response probability (0.40, 0.65 and 0.90), with response capacity limited to 500 alerts. At the reference threshold of 1.5, one 5%-prevalence, separation-2, no-drift condition yields mean residual hazardous opportunities of 180.8, 138.2 and 95.7 across the three response assumptions. With the same detector and nominal 65% response, imposing drift raises mean residual opportunities from 138.2 to 185.5. A sensitivity calculation also changes the preferred threshold when the relative weight of unresolved hazards and false alerts changes. The simulation shows why sensitivity, precision, workload and verified action belong in the same OHS decision model. All numerical data are computer-generated. The study does not report a deployed machine-learning system, workplace incidents, observed worker behaviour or injury reduction. Its contribution is a transparent stress test of the management choices that connect detection to prevention.

items.title: Opportunity in the Age of Agents: How Generative AI Changes Opportunity Recognition, Evaluation and Creation
items.abstract: Entrepreneurship theory explains how opportunities are recognised, evaluated and created, but it models every stage of that process as exclusively human. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now participates in all three stages: founders use large language models as co-ideators that generate opportunity candidates and as drafting partners that develop them, while investors use the same class of models to screen founders' submissions. This conceptual paper integrates opportunity theory (discovery, creation and effectuation) with the emerging empirical evidence on generative AI and ideation, creativity, evaluation and entrepreneurial performance. It argues that the co-ideator changes the opportunity process in four ways: it expands each founder's supply of candidates while compressing ideation skill gaps; it correlates opportunity pools across founders who draw on shared models, creating a homogenisation risk at market level; it raises the returns to prior knowledge, which governs selection among abundant machine-generated candidates; and it migrates durable advantage from generating opportunities to selecting, combining and enacting them. These claims are stated as seven formal propositions with boundary conditions, including the "jagged opportunity frontier" and the evaluation asymmetries produced by narrative AI explanations, with implications for founders, investors and educators, and a research agenda.

items.title: Organisational Conditions for Healthcare Workers' Wellbeing: The Roles of Leadership, Social Climate and Psychosocial Safety Climate
items.abstract: AIM: To assess a comprehensive model linking servant leadership, health-promoting leadership, workplace social climate, psychosocial safety climate, work conditions and healthcare workers' wellbeing. DESIGN: A cross-sectional survey design. METHODS: A total of 1563 healthcare workers completed a survey between 2024 and 2025. Structural equation modelling was employed to test the hypothesised relationships. RESULTS: Servant leadership, health-promoting leadership and workplace social climate were positively associated with healthcare workers' perceptions of psychosocial safety climate. Higher levels of psychosocial safety climate were linked to lower cognitive job demands and greater job resources, including job control, supervisor support and colleague support. These work conditions were associated with lower psychological strain and turnover intention, as well as higher job satisfaction and work engagement. Unexpectedly, cognitive job demands were positively related to work engagement, suggesting that cognitively challenging work may be perceived as meaningful and motivating in healthcare settings. CONCLUSIONS: Supportive leadership and a positive workplace social climate are important correlates of psychosocial safety climate, which was associated with healthier work conditions and better wellbeing among healthcare workers. In addition, the findings suggest that certain job demands may play a motivational as well as a straining role in healthcare contexts. IMPLICATIONS: Strengthening leadership practices and cultivating a supportive workplace social climate help healthcare organisations foster psychosocial safety climate and improve work conditions for healthcare workers. Enhancing these conditions supports healthcare workers' wellbeing and is associated with more sustainable healthcare workplaces. REPORTING METHOD: The STROBE checklist. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No patient or public contribution.

items.title: Patient-initiated conversational AI between appointments in breast cancer care: a multidisciplinary clinical and policy perspective
items.abstract: General-purpose conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for health-related questions, including questions relevant to cancer care, although breast-cancer-specific prevalence and behavioural effects remain poorly characterised. Most evaluations ask whether an AI answer is accurate. That is necessary but incomplete. Clinically consequential effects may arise when a fluent, apparently personalised exchange changes a treatment preference, delays contact with the clinical team, reinforces reassurance-seeking, validates non-adherence, or converts population guidance into an individual-sounding instruction. We conceptualise this as a parallel pathway: an AI-mediated sequence of questions, answers and actions that is usually invisible to the treating team, absent from the medical record and unattached to professional responsibility, yet capable of re-entering formal care through its downstream consequences. We distinguish model error from pathway error and propose traceability, reversibility, and returnability to accountable care as safety properties beyond answer accuracy. Across four clinical domains, we propose distinct pathway failure modes: premature preference closure in surgical decision-making; escalation closure during treatment toxicity; repetitive reassurance-seeking and over-reliance in psycho-oncology; and loss of conditionality in perioperative recovery and lifestyle advice. These are hypothesis-generating mechanisms rather than empirically established dominant patterns. We propose a five-step clinical response - ASK, RECONSTRUCT, CLASSIFY, CHECK and RETURN - based on non-judgemental inquiry, proportionate documentation and explicit return-to-care boundaries. Regulation can govern products and deployed systems, but it cannot by itself reveal patient-initiated consumer AI use. Clinical services therefore need governance for the pathway as well as for the technology.

items.title: Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in the AI era: a longitudinal reflexive thematic analysis of teacher reflective journals
items.abstract: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) lowers the threshold for producing work, not necessarily for learning. This study examines how an instructor kept an interdisciplinary AI course teachable for first-year art students, where that effort reached its limits, and how the instructor interpreted students' engagement with AI tools. Methods The study is a longitudinal practitioner self-study of a 12-week course taught in autumn 2025 at a higher vocational college in northwestern China. The data are the instructor's own reflective journals: structured entries written during the semester for Weeks 1–7 and retrospective accounts of Weeks 8–12 written after the semester ended. The two strata are reported separately. Reflexive thematic analysis produced 40 evidence anchors, five themes, one cross-cutting thread, and one central organizing theme, with a full audit trail. Results The instructor's repairs (translating content into everyday and discipline-specific tasks, working around broken or restricted lab equipment, and demonstrating on the teacher's computer) kept the course running. However, as content moved toward frontier tools that required paid accounts, computing resources, and prior AI experience, teaching drifted toward demonstration (“the more cutting-edge something is, the more it can only be demonstrated”). Across the semester the instructor recorded a recurring pattern, here termed a teacher-perceived low-threshold illusion , in which students appeared, in the instructor's account, to treat seeing, bookmarking, or one-click generation as equivalent to being able to do. The instructor associated this pattern with three co-occurring conditions: natural-language prompting and one-click generation, demonstration-only teaching, and a final assessment that students could complete without having attended. Participation could be high while, in the instructor's judgement, students gained little. Conclusion Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in AI teaching is bounded. Keeping an AI course running did not by itself make learning visible: the journals record a tension between engagement, product completion, and evidence of learning, not an established failure of learning. In-course repair reached limits shaped by access conditions and an inherited assessment format, and reconstruction of the course took place at the scale of the semester. We present pedagogical resilience reconstruction as an emerging construct for multi-case testing.

items.title: Pengaruh Video Pembelajaran Kreatif terhadap Motivasi Belajar Generasi Z dalam Pendidikan Sejarah Islam
items.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between creative learning videos and learning motivation among Generation Z students in the context of Islamic history education. Using a quantitative approach with correlational design, this research involved 30 students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using two main instruments: the Creative Learning Video Usage Questionnaire (CLVUQ) and Learning Motivation Scale (LMS), both demonstrating high reliability with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.906 and 0.942, respectively. The findings reveal a weak positive correlation (R = 0.340) between creative learning video usage and learning motivation, with an explanatory power of 11.6% (R Square = 0.116). A notably high acceptance rate of creative learning videos was reflected by 93.33% of respondents providing positive responses, with an average satisfaction score of 4.37 (SD = 0.62). Further analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation emerged as the most responsive dimension, with an average score of 4.12, compared to extrinsic motivation (3.89) and self-efficacy (4.01). These findings underscore the importance of integrating traditional and modern learning approaches in Islamic history education while emphasizing the need to consider contextual factors such as social, cultural, and institutional aspects in developing technology-based learning strategies. Despite certain methodological limitations, this research provides meaningful empirical foundations for developing more effective learning strategies in the digital era, particularly in the context of Islamic history education for Generation Z.

items.title: PERCEIVED INFLUENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON COMPUTATIONAL SKILLS AND MATHEMATICAL REASONING AMONG PRE-SERVICE TEACHERS IN NASARAWA STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study examined perceived influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on computational skills and independent reasoning among pre-service teachers in College of Education, Akwanga, Nasarawa State. Five research questions and three hypotheses guided the study. Descriptive survey design was adopted. Population was 125 NCE mathematics pre-service teachers, sample was 100 (62 males, 38 females) selected by simple random sampling. Instrument was Artificial Intelligence on Computational Skills and Mathematical Reasoning among Pre-Service Teachers (AI-CSMRPT) with reliability of 0.82 Cronbach Alpha. Mean and SD answered research questions, one-way ANOVA and one-sample t-test tested hypotheses at 0.05. Findings revealed AI significantly influences computational skills (Grand M=3.09) by improving speed (M=3.24) and accuracy (M=3.18). Both male (M=3.18) and female (M=2.95) agreed, but significant gender difference existed (F=4.67 > 3.94). AI also influences independent reasoning (Grand M=2.90), with reliance on AI before attempting problems (M=3.16) highest. Both genders agreed (M=2.98 male, M=2.77 female) with significant difference (F=4.12 > 3.94). No significant difference between influence on computational skills (M=3.09) and independent reasoning (M=2.90), p=0.47. Study concluded AI enhances computation but creates alternative cognition that reduces independent effort if unguided. Responsible and ethical use of AI as supplement, gender-sensitive training, and institutional guidelines were recommended.

items.title: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity
items.abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

items.title: PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Large Language Model Framework for Physics Data Analysis and Simulation
items.abstract: Abstract The inference of physical laws has traditionally relied on human intuition, analytical reasoning, and experimental observation. However, modern physics research is increasingly constrained by challenges such as high specialization, fragmented workflows, and limited computational resources, which impede scientific progress. To address these issues, we introduce PhysAgent , a novel multi-agent system powered by large language models (LLMs), designed to execute end-to-end scientific workflows—from hypothesis generation and computational modeling to data analysis and reporting. PhysAgent’s innovation lies in its specialized agent collaboration: a Mentor Agent guides scientific reasoning through Socratic questioning, a Student Agent handles technical execution (e.g., code implementation, DFT calculations), and a Leader Agent dynamically optimizes task scheduling and resource allocation. Integrating domain-specific tools like first-principles simulations (e.g., Quantum ESPRESSO, VASP), PhysAgent aims to improve reproducibility while maintaining human-in-the-loop refinement. We demonstrate PhysAgent as a proof-of-concept framework for recovering known physical relations from controlled data, including Kepler-law recovery from orbital trajectories and Newton-law recovery from force-motion data. Furthermore, it extends to ab initio materials modeling, automating electronic structure workflows (e.g., GaAs band-structure and density-of-states calculations). In addition, PhysAgent simulates complex real-world phenomena, such as raindrop flow on train windows. By harmonizing LLM-driven planning with domain-specific tools, PhysAgent provides a reproducible multi-agent workflow for physics data analysis and simulation. We provide a demonstration video of PhysAgent to illustrate its workflow and capabilities: https://b23.tv/emOilkC.
